Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The proposal asks for two changes from 1 June: raise the weekend Best Available Rate (BAR) from £145 to £165, and introduce a two-night minimum for stays that include a Saturday. It rests on three claims:

- last year's £10 rise was followed by higher occupancy, so guests aren't price sensitive;
- £204,000 is a *floor* on the extra revenue;
- the two-night minimum can only add to it.

I checked these against Table 1 and §§2–5. **The price-sensitivity evidence is confounded by seasonality, the revenue figure uses the wrong room count and applies the increase to rooms not sold at BAR, and the two-night minimum works against 38% of Saturday business.** A rate rise may still be right, but the case as written doesn't establish it.

## 1. The June-to-July comparison can't show price insensitivity

The £10 rise took effect in late June, and occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July. But §2 says July and August are the hotel's strongest months *because of* the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would have been expected to rise in July whatever the rate did. The comparison can't separate the price effect from the seasonal one, and July might have been higher still without the increase.

**What would settle it:** compare July to December 2025, priced at £145, with the same months of 2024 at £135. Better still, compare against how the competitive set's occupancy moved over the same months.

The 8.4 value-for-money score is real evidence that guests feel they get good value *at £145*. It suggests there is some room to raise prices. It can't tell you how they'll respond at £165, which is the lowest rate in the competitive set rather than £20 below it.

## 2. The revenue figure is overstated, so it isn't a floor

- **Room count:** §2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**, but §5 calculates on **124**. With 112 rooms: 112 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 ≈ **£184,000**.
- **Not every weekend room is sold at BAR.** Corporate rates, group rates and wedding blocks are all excluded from the increase. Weddings alone are 38% of Saturday-night bookings. If, say, 40% of weekend room-nights are sold off BAR, the gain falls to about £110,000.
- **Online travel agency commission** (typically 15–20%) comes off whatever share of the increase is booked through them.
- **Advance bookings at £145** for June onward will be honoured, so the first months will show less gain than a full year.

So £204,000 is a ceiling, not a floor. The realistic figure depends on the proportion of weekend nights sold at BAR, which the booking system can provide.

## 3. The two-night minimum may lose Saturday business

§4 records that **38% of Saturday room bookings are wedding guests who arrive Saturday and leave Sunday**. A two-night minimum applied to them would do one of three things:

- push them to book elsewhere;
- annoy them, and with them the couples and Quayside Hall, which is a significant referral source next door;
- or force exemptions, which the proposal doesn't mention.

"Group rates already contracted will be honoured" protects weddings that are already booked. It does nothing for future weddings, or for guests who book individually rather than through the couple's block.

More broadly, a minimum stay on a Saturday that *isn't* going to sell out mainly turns one-night bookings away. The 31 sell-out Saturdays show the minimum could work on those dates, but they are 31 of 52. The author treats the unquantified two-night effect as conservative upside. It could equally be a loss, which is another reason £204,000 isn't a floor.

**A more targeted approach:** apply the minimum only on dates forecast to sell out, and exempt wedding dates or wedding blocks.

## 4. Monitoring

Comparing pick-up week by week against the same weeks of 2025 is the right approach, because it controls for seasonality. On the five-point trigger:

- **Revenue break-even:** at £165, weekend occupancy can fall from 79% to about 69% before room revenue is lower than at £145 (79 × 145 / 165). That leaves roughly 10 points of headroom.
- **Spending beyond the room:** guests who don't come also don't spend on food, drink or parking. The real break-even is therefore tighter than 10 points, which makes a five-point trigger sensible.

It would also help to monitor the two-night minimum separately: track Saturday occupancy and wedding-guest bookings on their own. Otherwise losses there could be hidden behind the overall weekend figure.

## 5. What holds up

- **The hotel is priced below its competitive set.** £145 against £165–£180 is a genuine gap, and the 8.4 value score points the same way.
- **Saturday demand is constrained:** 31 sell-outs is real evidence of excess demand on those dates.
- **The arithmetic is correct on its own inputs** (124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 ≈ £204,000). The inputs are the problem.
- **Monitoring against the same weeks of 2025** is the right design.

## Recommendation for the proposal

1. **Correct the room count** to 112, and apply the £20 only to weekend nights sold at BAR, net of agency commission. Present the result as an estimate, not a floor.
2. **Replace the June-to-July evidence** with a year-on-year comparison against 2024, or with the competitive set's occupancy.
3. **Narrow the two-night minimum** to forecast sell-out Saturdays, with an exemption for wedding guests, and say how the Quayside Hall relationship will be handled.
4. **Consider varying the increase by date:** apply £165 on high-demand weekends first, and extend it once pick-up shows how guests respond.

A rate rise looks justified by the gap with competitors and the strength of Saturday demand. The proposal should rest on that, not on evidence that can't show what it claims.
